title: Temple Tax
summary: A Jewish payment associated with maintaining the Jerusalem temple, distinct from Roman tribute, customs tolls, voluntary offerings, and sacrificial purchases.
historical_context: Exodus 30:11-16 sets a half-shekel contribution for sanctuary service, and 2 Chronicles 24:4-14 narrates a collection to repair the temple. Matthew 17:24-27 presents collectors asking about the didrachma, while Mark 12:13-17 concerns tribute to Caesar. Read together, these passages help distinguish temple support from imperial taxation, but they do not by themselves establish how first-century collection operated across Judea and the diaspora.
ancient_near_east_context: The relevant setting is specific rather than a general ancient tax system: Exodus 30 and 2 Chronicles 24 describe sanctuary contributions, while Matthew 17 and Mark 12 portray distinct temple and Roman payment questions. The contrast clarifies the obligations named in each passage without supplying a full account of fiscal administration.
hebraic_worldview: The payment expresses corporate responsibility for sanctuary worship while remaining distinguishable from gifts, vows, and imperial taxation.
second_temple_context: Matthew 17's didrachma collectors presuppose a temple-associated payment; after 70 CE Rome redirected a Jewish tax to Jupiter Capitolinus, a later development not to be imported into Jesus's ministry.
canonical_context: Exodus provides the half-shekel precedent and Matthew 17 narrates a temple-tax dispute; Mark 12's tribute to Caesar concerns a different fiscal demand.
literary_context: Exodus 30 gives the half-shekel assessment; 2 Chronicles 24 narrates a repair collection; Matthew 17 stages a question about the didrachma and Jesus's response; Mark 12 separately stages the tribute-to-Caesar question. Reading these scenes side by side highlights distinct literary settings rather than one undifferentiated tax.
covenantal_significance: Temple Tax gives concrete form to divine presence among a holy people.
canonical_role: Temple Tax serves as an institutional anchor, connecting social practice, worship, leadership, and covenant life across related passages and themes.

related_objects.notes: The cluster distinguishes temple revenue from imperial tribute and toll collection.
